📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart complications, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

Recent findings suggest that they also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

Recent findings suggest that ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

In a recent development, we leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

It has been revealed that most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

According to recent reports, with a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

It has been revealed that on the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

Sources indicate that you may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Industry observers note that though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

Sources indicate that if you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

Sources indicate that for reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Sources indicate that ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

Recent findings suggest that during our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was swiftly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

According to recent reports, being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

In a recent development, the two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

According to recent reports, when push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

In a recent development, for an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Industry observers note that electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Sources indicate that similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#89071. These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1396 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.
  • A bigger animal comes with bigger parts.
  • In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.

A bigger animal comes with bigger parts. A massive dog has a big head, big paws, and a big tail, and the same goes for nearly every creature biologists have measured.

In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.

Their antennae come in the same sizes as the antennae of the much smaller workers, and the colony’s own chemical signals help shape how major each antenna grows.

A graduate student spotted it by accident under a microscope. Erica Vong, a researcher in Rajendhran Rajakumar’s lab at the University of Ottawa, showed him the antennae of two ants, and the smaller antenna belonged to the soldier.

“Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae,” noted Rajakumar, an associate professor in the university’s Department of Biology.

The ants belong to Pheidole, the big-headed ants. Each colony has two kinds of worker: small minors and much larger soldiers whose heads are about twice as wide.

Soldiers defend the nest and mill seeds, and workers do most of the rest.

Rajakumar’s team measured 100 workers and 100 soldiers of one Florida species, Pheidole dentata. For body size they used the width of the thorax just behind the head.

For the antenna they used its first segment, the long stalk that gives an ant’s antenna its elbow shape.

According to recent reports, soldiers had wider bodies and far wider heads, as expected. Their antenna stalks, though, were the same length on average as the workers’, and the whole antenna followed the same pattern.

The two castes’ measurements overlapped so completely that the team couldn’t tell them apart.

Recent findings suggest that within each caste the old rule still held. A bigger worker had a bigger antenna than a smaller worker, and the same was true among soldiers.

Pooled together, the numbers revealed no link between antenna and body at all, and the trend only reappeared once the castes were split apart.

Queens were the exception, with larger bodies and larger antennae than either worker caste.

To see whether one species was a fluke, the team pulled published measurements for 565 Pheidole species from the Americas.

Across the 565 species, soldiers and workers often had antenna stalks of similar length, even though soldiers consistently had wider heads.

Recent findings suggest that for each species, Rajakumar’s team divided the soldier’s antenna stalk by the worker’s. The most common answer was one, meaning no difference at all, with some species a little above and some a little below.

The same calculation for head width most often came out at 2 to 1, and no species came in under 1.4 to 1.

The team then measured ants from 14 other genera in three subfamilies, using live colonies, specimens from the Cornell University Insect Collection, and photographs from an online ant database.

In species with no soldier caste, and in most that evolved one on their own, antennae grew with the body as usual.

It has been revealed that the one exception was a turtle ant, Cephalotes varians, a close relative of Pheidole. The authors suggest the decoupling first appeared in the common ancestor the two groups share.

Recent findings suggest that whether a Pheidole larva becomes a worker or a soldier depends on how well it eats. A well-fed larva ends up with more juvenile hormone, and a high enough level turns it into a soldier.

Adult soldiers give off a pheromone that pushes the other way, so a colony with plenty of soldiers makes fewer latest ones.

The team tested both signals on larvae from lab colonies collected in Gainesville, Florida, and kept at 77°F (25°C) on a diet of mealworms and crickets.

They dabbed some larvae with a synthetic version of the hormone and raised each one with either two adult workers or two adult soldiers, starting with 40 larvae per condition.

The larvae were about a twentieth of an inch (1 to 1.5 millimeters) long, young enough that either fate was still open.

Hormone-treated larvae raised by workers became soldiers with a normal spread of antenna sizes.

Larvae raised by soldiers without the hormone became workers smaller than any found in a natural colony, with antennae to match. The team calls them nanoworkers.

“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” Rajakumar said.

“They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”.

Larvae that had already passed the point of no return toward becoming soldiers gave the stranger result.

Recent findings suggest that raised by soldiers, they emerged with soldier-sized heads on worker-sized bodies, and with antenna stalks shorter than those of the smallest natural workers. The team calls these nanosoldiers.

A developing soldier briefly grows a stub of a wing that never becomes a wing, and that stub acts as a signaling center that helps set the soldier’s significant head.

When the team switched off a gene that drives that stub, the larvae grew into smaller ants with smaller heads. Their antennae came out at nearly one size, with almost none of the usual spread.

The team has not found a nanoworker or a nanosoldier in the wild. The authors suspect selection weeds them out.

A soldier’s head on a worker’s body may not be properly supported, and an antenna that small may carry too few sensory hairs to do its job.

The authors also allow that the hidden potential could be a side effect of selection on something else, and the question of which is open.

Recent findings suggest that an ant’s antennae are its main contact with the world. They pick up trail and alarm pheromones, touch, heat, humidity, and vibration, and ants use them to tell nestmates from strangers.

Recent findings suggest that the elbow stalk matters too, because an ant swings it to aim the sensitive tip at whatever it is exploring. The stalk’s length sets where that elbow sits, which affects how an ant probes and follows a trail.

A longer antenna carries more sensory hairs, and earlier work found that how an ant responds to an intruder depends on how many of those hairs it has.

So a colony whose members span a range of antenna sizes may span a range of sensitivities as well.

Rajakumar’s team offers one explanation for why the two castes share a range. When a Pheidole colony runs short of workers, its soldiers take on worker jobs, including caring for young.

In a recent development, soldiers with the same spread of antenna sizes as workers may make that switch more easily. Once the next generation restores the balance, they can go back to defense.

“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Rajakumar said.

“In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”.

The authors wrote that the adaptive role of the decoupling is still unclear, and the job-switching idea is a hypothesis they haven’t tested.

Their hormone and pheromone experiments used one species, Pheidole dentata.

Roughly half the treated larvae died before reaching adulthood, which the authors attribute to raising each larva with only two adults instead of a full colony.

Antenna length was measured, not the sensory hairs on it, so whether a soldier’s small antenna senses what a worker’s does is still an open question.

Industry observers note that the evolutionary story also rests on a single turtle ant species. And 59 Pheidole species were left out of the genus-wide count because one caste or the other had no published measurement.

Checking the relatives is the next step the authors name.

If antennae turn out to be decoupled across the turtle ants and a third genus, Procryptocerus, the pattern would date back to the ancestor of all three.

Until someone measures those ants, the origin stays a hypothesis.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#89070. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday.
  • More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.
  • Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:.

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

Recent findings suggest that the outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a newly introduced map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

In a recent development, state and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the newly introduced lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

Recent findings suggest that the group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

According to recent reports, attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

It has been revealed that groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”.

Republican efforts to try again and enact a fresh congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

Industry observers note that the outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

Sources indicate that with over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”.

Industry observers note that the state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year. Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that presently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

Why are the spiral arms of this galaxy glowing?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.
  • A few bright white stars catch the eye first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.

Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.

A few bright white stars catch the eye first. Behind them, reddish clouds wind around a golden center, tracing the arms of a galaxy about 45 million light-years away.

The James Webb Space Telescope collected the data for this portrait in just 17 minutes of total exposure time.

What makes the image worth a longer look is how much is happening inside those arms.

The bright knots scattered along them show where young stars are already changing the clouds they formed from.

Elsewhere in the same galaxy, a massive star exploded in 2023, returning material to the space between stars.

The large white stars with long, sharp spikes belong to our own Milky Way.

They lie between Earth and NGC 2283 and appear in the picture because they happen to sit along Webb’s line of sight.

Their spikes come from the way light bends around parts of the telescope. Once you look past them, the galaxy’s shape is easier to pick out.

Two loosely wound arms curve away from an elongated band of stars that crosses the center.

Astronomers call that central structure a bar. Our own galaxy has one, too, but we observe the Milky Way from inside its disk.

Webb sees NGC 2283 almost face-on, giving us a clear view of how its bar and arms fit together.

Webb built this view from six exposures taken through different infrared filters.

Its Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument recorded different parts of the light coming from the same patch of sky.

According to recent reports, combining those observations lets astronomers see several things at once. Some filters pick up light from stars or from clouds of hydrogen energized by young stars.

Others detect the glow of carbon-rich molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are also found in soot on Earth.

Image processors assign visible colors to those infrared measurements.

The result lets us follow details that would otherwise be invisible to our eyes, including the uneven distribution of gas and dust along the arms.

The spiral arms look almost continuous from a distance. Look closer and they break up into bright clumps, wisps, and darker gaps.

The brightest knots include dense clouds of gas lit up by young stars.

In a recent development, A star begins forming when part of a cold cloud becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity. As material falls inward, the growing star heats up.

Some of the most massive young stars release enough ultraviolet light to energize the hydrogen around them, making the surrounding gas glow.

That glow gives astronomers a way to find places where star formation has happened recently.

In NGC 2283, the glowing clouds and young clusters make it possible to trace the arms even where dust hides some of the stars.

On January 28, 2023, astronomers discovered a supernova in NGC 2283.

Known as SN 2023AXU, it was a Type II supernova, the kind that can occur when a massive star runs out of fuel in its core.

Once the core can no longer support itself against gravity, it collapses. The resulting explosion throws the star’s outer layers into space.

Over time, material from explosions like this can mix with surrounding gas and become part of clouds that form latest stars.

That process changes the ingredients available to later generations.

Elements such as oxygen and sodium can travel far from the star that released them, then end up in another star or in the material that gathers around it.

NGC 2283 is one of 55 nearby galaxies Webb observed in a program designed to study how stars, gas, and dust interact.

These galaxies are close enough for Webb to distinguish individual star clusters and gas clouds, allowing astronomers to compare conditions from one part of a galaxy to another.

In this portrait, the spiral arms may be the first thing you notice. The small knots along them are what make the scene worth coming back to.

Each marks a place where young stars are already leaving a visible imprint on the material around them.

Industry observers note that image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Leroy.

Latest Update: Narwhals helped solve a mystery deep in Greenland’s fjords

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sensors carried by six narwhals highlighted warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.
  • Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.
  • Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sensors carried by six narwhals highlighted warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.

Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.

Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.

This matters because melting glaciers release freshwater into the North Atlantic. That water can change ocean layers, currents, and climate patterns far beyond Greenland.

Yet many East Greenland fjords are difficult to reach. Sea ice, harsh weather, and long distances often keep research ships away, leaving major gaps in ocean records.

It has been revealed that six narwhals have now helped fill some of those gaps in data from fjords. Sensors carried during their normal dives showed warmer Atlantic water reaching deep fjords and glacier fronts far inland.

Scoresby Sound lies on Greenland’s east coast and forms the world’s largest fjord system.

According to recent reports, fjords are long, narrow arms of the sea that reach deep into the land. Narwhals can move through fjord areas that ships rarely reach.

Professor Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen of the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources helped lead the work.

“The narwhals have been in parts of the fjords where very few measurements have been taken before. And there, 300 kilometers from the coast, we find traces of Atlantic water.

“It is completely new that we can show this,” mentioned Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Sources indicate that local hunters helped capture and tag six narwhals near Scoresby Sound. The tags measured water temperature, salt level, depth, and location for between 85 and 332 days.

Between 2017 and 2020, the animals collected 2,060 ocean profiles.

Each profile recorded water conditions at several depths during a dive, giving the team repeated readings from remote waters that ships rarely sample directly.

Some readings came from more than 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) below the surface.

Professor Susanne Ditlevsen of the University of Copenhagen helped analyze the large collection.

“Now we suddenly have measurements from places we can use in our models, giving us a much more complete picture of the ocean. It is absolutely fantastic to use the animals in this way,” mentioned Professor Ditlevsen.

In a recent development, east Greenland has cold Polar Water near the surface and warmer, saltier Atlantic water below it. Salinity simply means the amount of salt in water.

The team combined the narwhal readings with more than 2,200 older profiles from the World Ocean Database.

It then built a model, which is a math tool that finds patterns in large amounts of data.

“We used the two large datasets to build a robust model showing how temperature, salinity and depth are related,” explained Professor Ditlevsen.

“The models show that the layer consisting of Atlantic water has become thicker, while the upper layer of Polar Water has become thinner,” she added.

The results point to a stronger Atlantic influence in the region.

The Blosseville Basin warmed over the study period, with summer records showing warming in both the colder Polar Water and the warmer Atlantic water.

The shape of the seafloor controls where deep water can travel. Shallow ridges may block it, while deep channels can carry it toward glaciers.

Atlantic water became the main water type below about 820 feet (250 meters) in the Blosseville Basin.

It also crossed an underwater ridge and moved into the remote inner parts of Scoresby Sound.

The warmer water reached glacier basins about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from the coast.

Glaciers in deep basins faced warmer and saltier water than glaciers along the shallower Blosseville Coast.

Recent findings suggest that this shows why fjord depth matters. A glacier can sit far inland and still receive Atlantic water when a deep route connects it to the open sea.

The team compared ocean conditions with the amount of ice that broke away from glaciers. This process is called iceberg discharge.

Where water at 1,310 feet (400 meters) was warmer and saltier, icebergs accounted for a larger share of the glaciers’ total summer ice loss.

Sources indicate that “This is the water that helps melt the glaciers. We show how the warm water can contribute to accelerating the rate at which glaciers lose ice,” said Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Ocean heat can reach the ice from below, but the results do not show that warm water caused every change in glacier loss.

Air temperature, surface melting, seafloor shape, and local glacier conditions also matter, so the pattern does not point to one simple cause.

Only six narwhals carried sensors, and the animals chose their own routes.

Because narwhals prefer cold water, they may have spent less time in the warmer Atlantic layer.

The older ocean records were also uneven. Few measurements came from some fjords before 2010, so long-term changes inside Scoresby Sound remain difficult to judge.

The tags were not recovered after use. The team could not check them again for small changes in accuracy, especially in the salt readings.

Recent findings suggest that winter findings need extra care because narwhals provided most of the recent winter measurements. Their routes may not represent the whole region.

Climate models use real measurements to estimate how Earth may change.

Better ocean records can improve estimates of future glacier melt in Greenland, a point that Professor Ditlevsen connected to the larger climate question.

In a recent development, “In the large climate models used to predict future climate change, glacier melt plays a major role. That is why it is crucial that we improve our understanding of it, particularly because Greenland contains so much ice.”.

The newly introduced data can strengthen future climate estimates. Narwhals cannot replace ships, satellites, or long-term ocean stations, but they can reach waters that people struggle to measure.

Their dives revealed a clear route for warm Atlantic water into remote fjords.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

  • Robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. These intuitive little machines keep your floors tidy by vacuuming up dust, food crumbs, pet hair, and more—all without requiring you to lift a finger. They’re the ultimate “set it and forget it” cleaning solution because with robot vacuums, there’s no longer a need for you to lug around a heavy canister or upright vacuum.

Robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years. Today’s models are smarter, faster, and more capable than ever before. Many have the ability to map your home’s layout, create custom cleaning routines, and empty their own dustbins.

They’re also packed with sophisticated sensors to avoid stairs and furniture, dodge socks and dog toys, and skirt past other obstacles. Some models also include mopping functionality for complete floor care. And app and voice control allow you to start, stop, and schedule your vacuum to run from anywhere.

Below, we’ve gathered some valuable tips on what to look for in a robot vacuum and how to use these devices. Plus, find out how we tested the top robot vacuums and which one is best for you.

Industry observers note that for models that we tested in-house, we set up three 8-by-8-foot pens, each with a different floor surface, to simulate various cleaning scenarios for each robot vacuum. One pen featured low- to medium-pile carpet. The second had bare, polished concrete, and the third had laminate flooring. We set a stool, floor mat, and ottoman on the concrete to act as common obstacles found in the home.

In each pen, we also scattered flour, dried rice, and crushed up cereal to represent different types of dirt and detritus. This stress test pushed the vacuums beyond typical maintenance cleaning, so we could assess how they handle more material compared to an average encounter.

It has been revealed that to better understand how these robot vacuums functioned in everyday environments, we sent several models home with staff members and testers for real-world experience. This allowed us to confidently evaluate how each device handled household challenges like pet hair, kids’ messes, and varying floor types.

It has been revealed that our testers used the vacuums for a month or more, assessing them based on key criteria like features, cleaning effectiveness, navigation capability, ease of use, and overall value. Although these selections were not subjected to standardized lab testing, our recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience and long-term use.

Recent findings suggest that we are continuously refining this list to reflect the latest advancements in robot technology. Our ongoing updates show our commitment to providing trustworthy, up-to-date guidance and selections that are relevant. As new components are introduced and we test more models, we always carefully evaluate and incorporate these insights to help you choose the right tools for maintaining a clean and comfortable home.

We’ll soon be testing the Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum, which is an uprgraded version of our previous Best Overall recommendation, the Qrevo S. The latest model offers much of the same functionality, along with a few improvements—and a couple trade-offs.

Like its predecessor, the QV 35A is a dual system that both vacuums and mops, but it increases suction power up to 8,000 Pascals—1,000 more than the Qrevo S—for stronger cleaning performance. The spinning mop heads reach 200 rotations per minute and lift 10 millimeters, helping prevent carpets and area rugs from getting wet as the robot vacuum moves between thresholds. However, unlike the Qrevo S, the mop heads rely on air drying rather than using a hot air drying system, which could mean longer downtime between cleaning sessions.

Beyond cleaning performance, the QV 35A uses LiDAR navigation to scan and mop your home, creating detailed layouts within the companion app. It stores up to four floor plans, making it a practical option for multi-story households. The app also supports a range of customization features like scheduled cleanings, custom routes. and real-time machine monitoring.

Sources indicate that to support all of this, the highly capable docking station is designed for lower maintenance. It holds 2.7 liters of dry debris and 4 liters of water, allowing for several weeks of use before needing attention. Taken all together, these features suggest the QV 35A should perform similarly to the Qrevo S, which handled laminate, concrete, and medium-pile carpet effectively during our previous testing.

Full Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum Review.

Industry observers note that if you–or your pet–tend to shed a lot of hair, the Eureka J15 Pro robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. The base has a built-in, automatic hair cutting tool that slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have manually remove hair from the roller.

This robot vacuum isn’t lacking in power, either. It delivers 16,000 Pa suction for a deeper clean, and it works on a variety of floor types like carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile. The J15 Pro has advanced obstacle detection, and our tester, who has been using this model for months, tells us that it’s great at avoiding furniture, cords, pet toys, and over-friendly pets. It even takes a picture whenever it runs into something in its cleaning path, and you’re able to view the photo within the map afterwards in case it’s something that should be moved liked shoes and cords (or an animal).

The mopping feature is also effective at keeping your house clean. There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper clean, and they extend to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards. Our tester found the J15 Pro to be quiet on all modes, but Turbo is noticeably louder than the nighttime mode. You have control over suction power, though, so it doesn’t have to be running at full capacity constantly if you want to cut down on background noise.

In a recent development, she does mention that while this is a smart device and the app is advanced, it’s a little overwhelming to deal with. There are a plethora of settings and options available, and while it’s easy to set up basic settings initially, it gets a lot more involved. Those who are really just looking for daily maintenance and don’t want all the bells and whistles may find this cumbersome.

Full Eureka J15 Pro Robot Vacuum Review.

Recent findings suggest that as a first-time robot vacuum owner, our tester has been very pleased with his ongoing experience using the dreame X40 Ultra. It’s been able to take on dirt, dust, crumbs, and anything that his dog tracks inside, and exceeded expectations on hardwood floors. There are a few places it struggled to reach, like under a coffee table and TV stand, but we chalk that up to a height concern rather than capability concerns.

The X40 Ultra has 12,000 Pa of suction power, and a liftable, extendable side brush that gets close to wall corners and furniture legs. To protect rugs and carpets from getting wet, the robot vacuum either detaches the mop heads or lifts them to 10.5 millimeters, preventing any wet and dry mess combinations.

The app also allows you to program no-go zones, including rugs or other problem areas like staircases. Even with pet toys laying around the house, the X40 was able to navigate and map the layout with ease, all while avoiding these obstacles.

The mopping feature is a favorite for our tester. If you’re constantly on the go, having a robot vacuum capable of mopping on a daily basis is a real game changer. And thanks to auto-empty and auto-refill tanks, it’s really a set-it-and-forget-it device. We only suggest that you run the robot vacuum overnight so you aren’t disturbed by its run cycle. (Waking up to beautiful, clean floors is fun, too.).

Full Dreame X40 Ultra Robotic Vacuum Review.

Sources indicate that ecovacs has been around since the late 90’s, and the brand introduced its first Deebot in 2007. Needless to say, its designs have come along way, and one of the latest versions piqued our interest for one main reason: stain removal.

Most often, robot vacuums with mopping capability can only handle fresh spills on hardwood and tile, not the stubborn, dried-on stuff. The Deebot X12 is trying to change that. It uses an AI camera and infrared stain detector to identify spills, splatters, and even muddy paw prints. Then, it deploys two jets with cleaning solution at up to 46,000 Pascals to loosen residue for the mop roller head to pick up. This could potentially save you from having to make a more detailed pass by hand.

Industry observers note that the vacuum has capable power on carpet, too. It uses 22,000 Pascals of suction power to get rid or dirt, hair, and debris, and features an anti-tangle side and main brush to prevent hair from getting trapped around the bristles and roller.

In a recent development, the docking station is one of the more advanced designs we’ve seen in a robot vacuum. It has a bagless dustbin, power washing for the mop roller, and hot air drying. We’re looking forward to testing out this model and updating this guide accordingly with our findings.

Full Ecovacs Deebot X12 Omnicycle Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

The Qrevo CurvX is a newer design from Roborock, and we like that is has a slimmer build to fit under a wider variety of furniture, but still packs 22,000 Pa of suction power (the highest on our list). It’s equipped with a range of smart features, including pet recognition technology and two-way video calling (in the Roborock app) to interact with furry friends while you’re away, making it a great choice for households with animals.

The initial mapping process took a bit of time, but alas, this is a crucial step for an accurate layout of your home. Once the mapping was complete, the CurvX navigated efficiently, avoiding unnecessary paths and cleaning strategically as it went. During operation, the vacuum ran very quietly, especially when compared to other Roborock models we’ve experienced.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest conveniences is the automatic dustbin emptying system, as it significantly reduces the need for manual maintenance. The tanks hold debris for up to seven weeks, and the water tank automatically refills the reservoir on the robot vacuum so you don’t have to.

Industry observers note that the mop lifting and carpet detection performed well in our lab tests. When used in the concrete floor pen with obstacles like a small rug, it raised the heads with ease when transitioning between floor types. This ensured that carpets didn’t get wet during mopping sessions and the robot maintained the right cleaning mode. The edge mopping system is also a fantastic feature. The mop heads sit on arms that extend outwards for better reach, and they were able to get under and around table legs more efficiently.

That being said, this model isn’t without its limitations. In some of our mess tests, it missed detritus that was close to the pen walls, or “room edges,” despite the side brush kicking up the debris. It got closer than other robot vacuums we tested, but this is still a common struggle for many other models.

Full Roborock Qrevo CruvX Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

If you don’t need a robot vacuum with mopping capability, then the Shark PowerDetect is a viable option. It doesn’t sacrifice on features where you need them, and works well on different types of flooring.

Sources indicate that our tester found that the robot vacuum could clean various floor types and pick up after pets with ease. After after just one cycle, they noticed the difference.

The vacuum has one side brush, but since it rotates 360-degrees, it’s able to get close to baseboards and edges without leaving much of anything behind. The PowerDetect also does a great job of moving around obstacles. During testing, the vacuum got pretty close to a hair dryer cord to clean as much of the floor/carpet as possible, but it never tried to vacuum over it or got tangled.

Battery life held up too, and the robot vacuum was able to clean multiple rooms before returning to the docking station to charge. Our tester did note that the battery drains faster in Matrix Clean mode, but this isn’t completely unexpected because max suction requires more power.

According to recent reports, one of the first things that sets the Eufy Omni S2 is its unique docking station. Most robot vacuums on the market have tanks that are side by side and sit lower to the ground, but the S2’s docking station is taller and more narrow, making it easier to access to refill and empty (and find a place to store).

Another is suction power. The Omni S2 pulls at up to 30,000 Pa, and our tester noticed the difference immediately, especially in high-traffic spots that get flattened and dull over time. The 100 air watts of consistent airflow was able to pull in dirt, allergens, and pet hair from deep between carpet fibers instead of just picking up debris from the surface.

The S2 uses a DuoSpiral main brush, which is actually two separate brush rolls with a gap in the middle to funnel hair into the suction port to prevent tangles, and it has proven reliable in a household with six pets.

Most mopping robot vacuums use spinning mop heads to clean your floors, but the Omni S2 uses a rolling mop with electrolyzed water and plenty of downward pressure for an even clean. The main downside is there is no option for mopping-only or vacuum-then-mopping cleaning modes. Many of our other recommendations are able to do these processes separately, so it’s definitely something to consider. The base station takes care of much of the dirty maintenance work, including self-emptying, self-refilling, hot water washing and hot air drying of the mop roller.

Full Eufy Omni S2 Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

Many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. As a result, we’re often adding and swapping out our recommendations in this list. Here are a few other robot vacuums we’ve tested that still warrant recognition:.

Eufy X10 Pro Omni Robot Vacuum and Mop: This combination robot vacuum and mop reduces monotonous upkeep tasks with carefully curated features. The docking station lasts for up to 60 days before needing attention, and other key highlights include auto-refill, auto-wash, self-dry, and self-emptying to make maintenance virtually hands-free.

In a recent development, roborock Curv Flow 2 Robot Vacuum and Mop: The Roborock CurvX we recommend above is the stronger all-around robot vacuum, but the Curv Flow 2 is a good alternative if you want a mop roller that continuously refreshes itself with clean water to prevent dirty mop drag. This robot vacuum is also rated for up to 20,000Pa of suction power, has a larger dustbin, and performs well on hard floors.

Recent findings suggest that navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR).

It has been revealed that this navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

With this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM).

In a recent development, this triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

According to recent reports, suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each fresh model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

In a recent development, A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for major homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Recent findings suggest that beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

The most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

Sources indicate that throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

In a recent development, look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Industry observers note that most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

In a recent development, when set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

For homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

Sources indicate that amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," stated Rep.
  • A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.
  • Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond promptly to cybersecurity and other threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," stated Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond promptly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

According to recent reports, the legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

In a recent development, “With advances in AI creating upcoming cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more vital than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster stated in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”.

Recent findings suggest that foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI challenges on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the latest Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking noted.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a manufacturer that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

Industry observers note that he's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

Industry observers note that “He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking mentioned. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

Recent findings suggest that the draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the problem at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary states.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

Industry News: Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A new map offers surprises

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation prepares based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.
  • Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.
  • A fresh global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation prepares based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A fresh global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

Across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

Recent findings suggest that europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

It has been revealed that in the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

Industry observers note that global averages hide substantial differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

Freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he remarked.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant said.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles indicated the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

The hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

Recent findings suggest that “What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he stated.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into looks explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

It has been revealed that the maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

In a recent development, asked which places he would look at first, Brabant mentioned threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that what would help most right now, he noted, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it
