What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, notes Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • It has been revealed that their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, notes Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

It has been revealed that their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium demonstrated they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data showed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

Industry observers note that “That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy claims. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

According to recent reports, the number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

Sources indicate that researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” claims José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” says Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

SpaceX introduced its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

For decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

It has been revealed that historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

Operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he claims, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

Recent findings suggest that aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

Injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering aims. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

“The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy states. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

Industry observers note that one reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

According to recent reports, to quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are currently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross says. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

It has been revealed that to do better, scientists are developing upcoming models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

But state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

Sources indicate that to validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens says. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

Since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens indicates.

According to recent reports, but in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — launched in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

Recent findings suggest that “We could get close,” Lemmens says. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens says. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

In a recent development, on Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

According to recent reports, the team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

In a recent development, altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency looks to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” indicates Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens claims.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

If research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” says Ross.

After scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

In a recent development, still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he notes.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

Some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, noted at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

Recent findings suggest that “I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur stated, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks currently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, remarked at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, rolled out to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

Ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he says, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” noted Young.

A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that presently defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell notes.

Recent findings suggest that can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Kate Wheeling is a freelance journalist based in Santa Barbara, California. She writes about the environment and humans’ relationship with the natural world. Her work has appeared in The Atlantic, Smithsonian magazine, The Daily Beast, and Mother Jones.

‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer.
  • After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.
  • Industry observers note that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

Industry observers note that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted on Monday evening.

In a recent development, asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

In a recent development, “Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I stated, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy mentioned Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

It has been revealed that in the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, remarked she has seen such requests debuted in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

It has been revealed that and several Senate GOP aides noted that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

Recent findings suggest that republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick noted in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday remarked the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he remarked, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

Latest Update: The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • Industry observers note that in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

Industry observers note that in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Sources indicate that saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Recent findings suggest that located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Industry observers note that pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — currently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

It has been revealed that sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

Industry observers note that sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

Recent findings suggest that zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

It has been revealed that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so substantial and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

According to recent reports, the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

In a recent development, thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

Industry observers note that by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

It has been revealed that friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

You’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

While you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

Clean indoor air has become more crucial than ever. While allergens like dust, dander, mold, and bacteria are all teaming up to infiltrate the air you breathe, the widespread wildfire smoke affecting much of the U.S. right now is also proving just how promptly outdoor pollution can make its way inside. According to the EPA, Americans spend about 90 percent of their time indoors, where pollutant concentrations can sometimes be even higher than they are outside. An air purifier protects your airways from airborne irritants while providing clean, fresh air indoors (which is why we think everyone should invest in an air purifier).

We got our hands on air purifiers from brands like Coway, Levoit, and GermGuardian and put them to the test. Filtration was our main concern, so we could determine the air purifiers’ efficiency. Then we moved along to other factors such as noise while running, how well they work in a given room, and convenience features. After our in-home testing, these are the air purifiers that came out on top.

We tried out several air purifiers with a range of filtration systems, noise levels, and features. We tested these models in multiple different apartments, placing them in various rooms of the home to measure their efficiency. We considered the different uses of an air purifier, like if you’re an allergy sufferer or have a home filled with furry friends, and tested special features like light-up displays and automatic shutoff to determine their ease of use and effectiveness. We considered the amount of time it took to set up the different purifiers and install their filter systems.

For units that we haven’t tested, we combed through dozens of potential products and their specifications, reviews, and user complaints to identify what we thought were the best air purifiers. We settled on the following list, which includes options that are budget-friendly, sleekly designed, and high-performing.

Industry observers note that the Airmega Mighty2 is the latest version of our previous Best Overall pick, the Coway AP-1512HH. The newest model combines power, quality filters, and robust controls to help you breathe easier.

Industry observers note that the Mighty2 uses a three-stage filtration system to capture 99.7 percent of airborne particles, and cleans spaces up to 1,800 square feet in 60 minutes. It has three standard fan speeds, but there’s a turbo mode that will kick on if there’s a big uptick of matter in the air.

The original version just used an indicator light system that let you know basic air quality levels, but this updated model has a built-in air quality index sensor that measures and displays particulate matter counts in real time.

In a recent development, our tester tried the air purifier in his New York apartment, putting it up against pet odors, litterbox dust, and other household allergens. “Results after about a day were already noticeable. The air in the room seemed clearer and there was less dust on the ground in the area immediately around the litterbox. Not enough that I’m going to have to sweep up any less, mind you, but there was a material difference that I wasn’t getting from using a smaller purifier.”.

This air purifier from Clorox uses a three-stage filtration system to trap allergens, pollutants, and VOCs, and it successfully cleared strong scents and odors from the apartment we tested in.

In a recent development, if you’re a pet owner, specifically with cats, then you know that the litter box smell lingers long after your little fur ball has left the lavatory. The Vital 200S-P from Levoit is a great way to combat the odors that candles and air fresheners just can’t cover up. I set the air purifier up in my living room and noticed a clear improvement in scent after running for the day.

Recent findings suggest that this unit has a traditional air inlet, along with a unique U-shaped inlet that is ideal for trapping pet hair without clogging up the filters. If you pair your air purifier with the app and select Pet Mode, it automatically alternates between fan speeds, too. The pre-filter is easy to remove and wash, so you don't have to purchase replacements as often.

Industry observers note that since we tested the Vital 200S-P in a smaller apartment, it was a bit obtrusive. But the air purifier covers up to 1,875 square feet, so if you live in a townhouse or single-family home, this unit will accommodate.

It has been revealed that the Airmega 100 is the first cylindrical unit in the Coway line, which is a nice switch-up from the rectangular model that we tested in the past. It tucked nicely into the corner of the living room, and you can change the light between blue, orange, and off, which is ideal if you’re using the purifier in a bedroom.

According to recent reports, I tried the fan on various settings, and the lowest mode could barely be heard over the TV playing at an average volume, which aligns with its claimed 20-decibel noise level. You can manually adjust everything on the control panel, or let the purifier do its thing and adapt accordingly as it monitors the air quality of the room.

Setup of the unit was simple; you essentially just need to click the filter into place. This model uses a 3-in-1 filtration system, with a HEPA filter sandwiched between a vacuumable pre-filter and deodorizing filter. The deodorizer layer is especially useful if you have pets, love to cook, or live in an apartment or complex with odors.

Full Coway Airmega 100 Air Purifier Review.

According to recent reports, for smaller rooms or office spaces, the smart Blueair 511i Max offers much of the same performance and features as larger, more capable models. It only purifies areas of up to 465 square feet, but does so within just 30 minutes on the highest setting. The three-layer filtration system captures up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles, too.

We appreciate that the air quality level is clearly displayed on the front in a five-color scale, and that the display has auto-brightness controls if you're running it overnight while you're sleeping. Advanced features are available through the app, including scheduling and air quality reports.

This unit has a four-stage filtration system, along with Blueair's proprietary HEPASilent filter that uses a combination of electrostatic charge and mechanical filtration to capture 99.97 percent of airborne pollutants and contaminants. This type of filtration technology is less dense than other filter options, so it's designed to run quieter and use less energy.

The value offered by such a small air purifier is unmatched, considering it targets both allergens and odors—all with relatively quiet operation.

In a recent development, if you have a large space or even an entire apartment that needs air purification, the Coway Airmega 400 is the smart model you need. It's designed to cover up to 1,560 square feet in 30 minutes, and has a variety of smart features and sleep settings, all packed into a compact yet capable unit. While this is the most expensive option we recommend, it's relatively affordable considering its capacity, and you shouldn’t have to supplement with an additional air purifier.

It’s surprisingly quiet given its size, reaching only 22 decibels on its lowest setting. We like that it uses multi-stage purification methods, combining a pre-filter, an activated carbon filter, and a True HEPA filter to capture the tiniest of particles. The pre-filter is washable, but the air filter indicator light will let you know when it actually needs to be replaced.

It has been revealed that the Airmega 400 has a three-setting smart mode that adapts to its environment, with a fan speed that automatically adjusts based on air quality or lighting conditions. We also appreciate the option to use eco mode, which turns the fan on and off when the room has remained purified for 30 minutes, and there’s also a timer and pollution sensor.

The GermGuardian isn’t a flashy design with robust features, but it aids in keeping the air in my apartment free of pet odors, dust, and smoke.

Sources indicate that I have a self-cleaning litter box, which significantly cuts down on smells and dust associated with cat waste, but it doesn’t solve every problem. I let the purifier run during one of the Litter Robot’s cleaning cycles, and thanks to the GermGuardian’s built-in air quality index (AQI) sensor and display screen, I was able to see the particulate matter count in the air reach triple digits in seconds. The automatic fan speed varied as needed, and it wasn’t long before air quality was back to a healthy level.

I put the GermGuardian up against incense smoke, too, and it went to work swiftly. The fan had to run at high speed for longer, but by the end, my living room was clear of any lingering haze and odor.

Industry observers note that in addition to a HEPA filter and activated carbon, this model also has a UVC light, which is claimed to disinfect bacteria, viruses, and mold. While I did give this feature a try, I didn’t keep it on for long because it’s hard to prove whether these lights are actually useful in an air purifier.

The Sans HEPA 13 air purifier offers quiet operation, whole-home purification, and smart features. This unit runs at only 25 decibels on the lowest fan setting, and I could hardly tell that it was on, even when standing next to the unit.

It has been revealed that the air purifier is best used for whole-home use, as it purifies spaces up to 1,854 square feet. The internal sensors monitor and show you the air quality index in real time, and the reading is visible on the touch display. I’m able to view PM2.5, which is particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller, such as dust, smoke, pollen, and pet dander, as well as PM10, which are slightly larger particles up to 10 microns, like coarser dust and mold spores.

Sources indicate that this unit pairs a medical-grade HEPA 13 filter with a pre-filter, activated carbon filter, and UV-C light to capture 99.9 percent of particles. This might be overkill for general household use, but I’ve appreciated the multi-stage approach. The only downside I’ve come across is that overall cost will likely be higher, considering the Sans recommends replacing the filter every three months.

There is no shortage of air purifiers on the market, and many of them use a lot of the same tech to achieve better air quality. We’re often testing many different models to find the top recommendations. Ahead are some that haven’t made it to this roundup, but are still worth considering.

Industry observers note that rabbit Air A3 Air Purifier: This air purifier uses a six-stage filtration system to rid your home of smoke, dander, odors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and germs. The lowest fan setting clocks in around 20 decibels, which is extremely quiet, so you can run this model daily without being disturbed. The build is relatively bulky so it’s not the easiest to tuck into a corner and out of the way, and the $760 price tag is pretty steep.

GermGuardian AirSafe+ XL: This model is shaped like our best portable pick above, and comes with a lot of the same features as the other GermGuardian we recommend, and it has a companion app for tracking air quality metrics. That stated, the app doesn’t specify what type or size particulate matter the sensor is measuring, so it’s hard to tell what common allergens are actually floating around your home.

Air purifiers vary in filtration range, so it's important to first consider your room size before buying. To find a model that accommodates your space, the EPA recommends that you first multiply the length and width of the area where you intend to operate the air purifier to calculate the square footage.

Most air purifiers have a maximum coverage area listed, so just compare to your calculations to find an air purifier that is the best fit for your home.

If you have an open floor plan or high ceilings, opt for an air purifier with more coverage. You should also place the air purifier in the room you use most regularly, and make sure it’s in an area where the airflow isn’t obstructed.

The filter system of your air purifier might differ depending on the model and issue you're trying to target such as allergy relief, odor elimination, or germ protection. You’ll often see three-stage filtration (or four-, five-, or six-stage), which includes all three of the filter types detailed below.

Pre-filters are typically the first line of defense in an air purifier and trap larger particles like dust, hair, and fur, which helps extend the lifespan of the main filter and improves the overall efficiency of the unit.

All of our selections on this list involve a multi-step filtration system to target a majority of common pollutants and allergens in your household.

Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with NYU Langone Health, recommends selecting an air purifier that comes with a HEPA filter. “Make sure it's a HEPA air purifier since these filter down to 0.3 microns and have a robust amount of studies done showing their efficacy.” HEPA filters remove at least 99.97 percent of airborne particles like dust, bacteria, and pollen, and are the gold standard for air purification.

Recent findings suggest that activated carbon filters are more porous and help get rid of gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are commonly found in household items like surface cleaners and candles. These filters absorb molecules onto carbon and are best used in environments with strong odors or smoke.

With laundry machines, dishwashers, and fans all emitting their own noise, adding another loud appliance into the mix could be overkill, especially since air purifiers are meant to run the entire day.

Recent findings suggest that look for models that range from 10 to 30 decibels. A whisper is around 30 decibels, so expect air purifiers in this noise range to be almost virtually silent.

“Air purifiers need to be kept clean, and filters should be changed every six months,” Parikh states. Since air purifier filters are designed to collect and trap different-sized particles, contaminants, and hair, they get gunky pretty easily. This buildup could even reduce the efficiency and the air quality of the purifier if not cleaned often enough. Most air purifiers come with reusable filters, so just rinse them off in between replacements.

App compatibility, savvy control panels, remotes, check filter indicators, and variable settings are beneficial features that make it easier to use your air purifier. If you want to monitor the air quality levels in your home or keep tabs on filter life, look for an air purifier that pairs with an app. If you’re easily overstimulated by loud noises, consider an air purifier that has different modes for adjusting the speed of the internal fan.

In a recent development, air purifiers use a fan to draw air into the unit, then pass it through a series of filters to remove particles and contaminants. Said filters vary in effectiveness and normally target a specific concern like odors, smoke, and viruses. Once the air has passed through the fan and all of the appropriate filters, it is recirculated back into the room for a cleaner and healthier environment.

“Air purifiers filter out pollutants, improve air quality, remove infectious agents and pollen,” says Parikh. “They limit your level of exposure and reduce lung damage and flare-ups of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, and heart issues.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It can affect everyone’s health by causing inflammation and lung damage over time that may be either reversible or irreversible,” Parikh claims. “It is especially dangerous for those with underlying heart disease, lung disease, pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals.”.

A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations.
  • Recent findings suggest that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” states the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

Recent findings suggest that “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” states the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Sources indicate that would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, claims Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

According to recent reports, smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

According to recent reports, there are many ways a heart can grow, states Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Industry observers note that some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand claims, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

Recent findings suggest that stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

According to recent reports, there is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too major to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson claims. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Recent findings suggest that pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as significant as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that looking for a sky event this week?
  • The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • Recent findings suggest that from the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Recent findings suggest that from the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

In a recent development, asteroid 6993 (1995 BJ4), a small body 7 miles (11 kilometers) across, orbits in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. In August 2026, astronomers spotted a faint tail, making it candidate for the largest known main-belt comet. However, the tail has been gradually fading through 2026, which hints at it being caused by debris from a one-time impact rather than ongoing outgassing, astronomers reported last month in a paper accepted in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. In this image, the tail spans more than 35′, or wider than the Full Moon.

Latest Update: New Congress will still be filled with losers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct.
  • OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.
  • It has been revealed that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

It has been revealed that this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

It has been revealed that “We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown revealed his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

Sources indicate that the fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

In a recent development, republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Sources indicate that republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Upcoming Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

Industry News: The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
